subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Vmax represents:
options: the rate of reaction at zero substrate
the substrate concentration at which the enzyme denatures
the maximum rate of reaction when all active sites are saturated with substrate
the optimum temperature for the enzyme
questions.explain: Vmax is the theoretical maximum rate achieved when enzyme active sites are fully saturated and working at capacity.

questions.q: The rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction is usually measured as the INITIAL rate because:
options: temperature is highest at the start
at the start substrate is plentiful and not yet limiting, giving the true maximum rate for those conditions
the enzyme is most denatured at the start
questions.explain: Initial rate is measured before substrate depletion or product accumulation slow the reaction, giving a valid comparison of conditions.

questions.q: On a rate-against-substrate-concentration graph, increasing the concentration of a COMPETITIVE inhibitor would:
options: increase the substrate concentration needed to reach the same rate, but Vmax is still attainable
lower the Vmax that can be reached
have no effect on the curve
prevent Vmax ever being reached even at infinite substrate
questions.explain: Competitive inhibition can be overcome by sufficient substrate, so Vmax is unchanged but more substrate is needed to approach it.

questions.q: On a hot, sunny day a plant's rate of photosynthesis levels off and does not rise with further light. Which factor is most likely limiting?
questions.explain: When light is already plentiful, CO2 concentration commonly becomes the limiting factor that caps the rate.

questions.q: When an enzyme is immobilised by entrapment in alginate beads, the rate of reaction may be slightly lower than for free enzyme because:
options: the optimum temperature falls to 0 C
the substrate must diffuse into the bead to reach the active sites, slowing the reaction
questions.explain: Entrapment can hinder substrate access as it must diffuse through the matrix, though immobilisation still allows reuse and greater stability.

questions.q: Which two products of the light-dependent reactions are required by the Calvin cycle?
questions.explain: The Calvin cycle uses ATP for energy and reduced NADP to reduce GP to triose phosphate.

questions.q: Why does the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction typically decrease over time when measured as product formed?
options: Substrate concentration falls as it is converted to product, reducing collision frequency
The activation energy increases over time
The enzyme is denatured by the product
questions.explain: As substrate is depleted, fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form per unit time, so the rate declines until substrate runs out.

questions.q: A non-competitive inhibitor that binds reversibly to an allosteric site will, on a rate-against-substrate graph, produce:
options: an unchanged Km but a reduced Vmax
a reduced Km and unchanged Vmax
questions.explain: Because substrate binding is unaffected, Km stays the same, but fewer functional enzymes mean a lower maximum rate, so Vmax falls.

questions.q: If light intensity is suddenly reduced to darkness, what happens to the level of GP in the Calvin cycle?
options: It is immediately converted to RuBP
It rises because there is no reduced NADP or ATP to convert it to TP
It falls because no more CO2 is fixed
questions.explain: Without light, ATP and reduced NADP run out, so GP can no longer be reduced to TP and GP accumulates.

questions.q: Many enzymes require a cofactor such as a metal ion (e.g. Zn2+ or Cl-) because the cofactor:
options: is a non-protein component needed for the enzyme to function
denatures the enzyme to expose the active site
questions.explain: Cofactors are non-protein helpers required for catalytic activity, sometimes altering the active site shape to allow binding.

questions.q: A coenzyme differs from a prosthetic group in that a coenzyme:
options: is a small organic molecule that binds temporarily and is often derived from vitamins
is part of the protein's primary structure
is a permanently bound metal ion
questions.explain: Coenzymes are loosely bound organic molecules, frequently vitamin-derived, that participate transiently, unlike permanently bound prosthetic groups.

questions.q: At high substrate concentration with fixed enzyme concentration, the rate of reaction plateaus because:
options: all active sites are occupied so enzyme concentration becomes the limiting factor
questions.explain: When substrate is in excess, every active site is continually occupied, so the number of enzyme molecules limits the rate.

questions.q: A respiratory substrate gives a respiratory quotient (RQ) of about 0.7. Which substrate is most likely being respired?
questions.explain: Lipids are highly reduced and require more oxygen relative to CO2 produced, giving an RQ around 0.7.

questions.q: A prosthetic group differs from a coenzyme in that a prosthetic group is:
options: a permanently and tightly bound non-protein component of the enzyme
always an inorganic metal ion in solution
questions.explain: A prosthetic group is permanently bound to the enzyme (e.g. FAD in some dehydrogenases), unlike a coenzyme which associates only transiently.

questions.q: When a protein is used as a respiratory substrate, its amino groups must first be removed by which process?
questions.explain: Deamination removes the amino group from amino acids so the remaining carbon skeleton can enter respiration.

questions.q: During non-cyclic photophosphorylation, what is the final electron acceptor that becomes reduced?
questions.explain: At the end of the non-cyclic pathway, electrons and protons reduce NADP to reduced NADP for use in the Calvin cycle.

questions.q: According to the chemiosmotic theory, what directly drives ATP synthesis during oxidative phosphorylation?
options: Movement of protons down their electrochemical gradient through ATP synthase
Direct transfer of a phosphate from a substrate
Reduction of NAD by dehydrogenase enzymes
questions.explain: Protons flow back into the matrix through ATP synthase, and this flux powers the phosphorylation of ADP.

questions.q: As a proton gradient is generated across the inner mitochondrial membrane, where do protons accumulate?
questions.explain: Electron carriers pump protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space, building the electrochemical gradient.

questions.q: When investigating the effect of substrate concentration on enzyme rate, why is it important to use a buffer solution?
options: to keep pH constant so that pH does not act as an uncontrolled variable affecting the active site
to act as a competitive inhibitor
questions.explain: A buffer maintains constant pH, controlling a variable that would otherwise alter the enzyme's tertiary structure and confound results.

questions.q: In glycolysis, the six-carbon hexose bisphosphate is split to form two molecules of which three-carbon compound?
questions.explain: Hexose bisphosphate is lysed into two molecules of triose phosphate, each of which is then oxidised to pyruvate.

questions.q: In the Krebs cycle, the regeneration of the 4-carbon acceptor molecule allows the cycle to:
options: Stop after one acetyl group is processed
Continuously accept further acetyl CoA molecules
Produce oxygen for the electron transport chain
questions.explain: Regenerating oxaloacetate means the cycle can keep accepting new acetyl groups, turning repeatedly as respiration continues.

questions.q: In which cellular location does glycolysis occur, and which type of phosphorylation produces its ATP?
questions.explain: Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm and generates ATP directly by substrate-level phosphorylation.

questions.q: In the Calvin cycle, which enzyme catalyses the fixation of carbon dioxide onto RuBP?
questions.explain: RuBisCO catalyses the combination of CO2 with ribulose bisphosphate to form two molecules of GP.

questions.q: What is the NET yield of ATP from one molecule of glucose during glycolysis alone?
questions.explain: Four ATP are produced but two are invested in the early phosphorylation steps, giving a net gain of two ATP.

questions.q: What is the immediate source of the electrons that replace those lost from photosystem II during non-cyclic photophosphorylation?
questions.explain: Photolysis splits water, supplying electrons to photosystem II as well as protons and oxygen.

questions.q: In one turn of the Krebs cycle, how many molecules of reduced NAD, reduced FAD and ATP are produced respectively?
questions.explain: Each Krebs turn yields three reduced NAD, one reduced FAD and one ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation.

questions.q: A small mammal consumes 10 cm3 of oxygen and produces 8 cm3 of carbon dioxide in the same period. What is its respiratory quotient?
questions.explain: RQ = CO2 produced / O2 consumed = 8 / 10 = 0.8.

questions.q: Which is the correct order of stages in aerobic respiration?
options: Glycolysis then link reaction then Krebs cycle then oxidative phosphorylation
Krebs cycle then glycolysis then oxidative phosphorylation then link reaction
Link reaction then glycolysis then Krebs cycle then oxidative phosphorylation
Glycolysis then Krebs cycle then link reaction then oxidative phosphorylation
questions.explain: Glucose is split in glycolysis, pyruvate enters the link reaction, then the Krebs cycle, then oxidative phosphorylation.

questions.q: How many carbon atoms are in the citrate molecule formed when acetyl CoA combines with oxaloacetate in the Krebs cycle?
questions.explain: A 2-carbon acetyl group joins a 4-carbon oxaloacetate to form 6-carbon citrate at the start of the Krebs cycle.

questions.q: Which molecule is phosphorylated using ATP at the start of glycolysis, before the sugar is split?
questions.explain: Glucose is first phosphorylated to glucose phosphate, making it more reactive before it is split into two triose phosphates.
